comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
I first discovered Ross Douthat’s columns in my freshman year of college where I was gifted a free New York Times subscription. At that time I was excited for the bright progressive era under President Biden and annoyed with Douthat’s critiques. But then as Biden began to flounder and the country did not come together, I began paying attention to the internal contradictions of the liberal worldview that Ross drew attention to. The angst of a world with falling birthrates. The arbitrariness of which we call some groups oppressed and others oppressors. And finally the impossibility of solving our political problems through technocratic economics and technology without a moral center (and maybe Christianity has something to say in that regard.) 
It left me, if not a Republican, at least more small-c conservative. So thank you Ross for being my first exposure to intellegent conservative thought and best of luck in your next stage in life.

comments.name: Vanessa
comments.location: The woods on the periphery of the Ozarks
comments.body:
Unknown things? One of those unknown things Ross seems to think he understands is something he didn't live through, and that the "McCarthyite experience."  Maybe that's why he truly doesn't understand who the bad guys are. I hope he's not one of them, but I've begun to wonder.

Good luck with CBS, Ross. You're gonna need it.

comments.name: Meg L
comments.body: As for how ‘easily’ Trump policies can be rolled back, I think about hundreds of people blown up in boats in the Caribbean, tens of thousands dead without USAID, people killed by ICE, babies and children in detention right now, women who’ve died by being denied miscarriage treatment. Not fixable. At all.

comments.name: Chris Croom
comments.body: Look for uniters vs. dividers, and you will find the good guys and bad guys. Also, there's a lot of dualism in this piece when so much of the world is slightly different shades of morally gray. Moreover, both authoritarian/fascists and socialist/communists are forms of populism, and both strains of extremism are against what are supposed to be our values as a society. Finally, what we've learned since 2016 is trust not in one particular party to balance the budget, as our political system has rotted. Do however, trust that a lot of Americans on the fringes want to put other Americans they perceive to be on the opposite fringes in camps or jail, or have them deported. Licensing xenophobia causes this.

comments.name: BlueIguana
comments.body: The Bad Guys are winning.  Todd Blanche, President Trump's former personal attorney was just confirmed as Attorney General by two votes in the Senate.  We know who the Bad Guys are.   The Good guys were pipped at the post.

comments.name: Commenter
comments.body: Honestly, welcome to the world conservatism made. Sure, there was a woke interlude which one could frame as a reaction to the vileness of Trump and conservatism, but one should never lose sight of the fact that we live in a conservative world now and it’s really quite unbearable. Runaway capitalism, billionaires, Environmental collapse, lying, the end of expertise, morality being replaced with simplistic religious doctrine. the list goes on. This is the world conservatism made. So much for the Reagan revolution.

comments.name: Theodore S.
comments.body: Many thanks Ross, for explaining why “There Will Be No Trump Coup” in October 2024.  Yes, it’s so difficult to know the difference between the good guys and the bad guys.

comments.name: TH Black
comments.body: Makes complete sense RD is headed to 60 Minutes. Will he be able to illuminate the darkness that enshrouds that once light-giving show or will he be a part of its slide into irrelevance? Interesting Times taught me to listen to people whose views have been a part of our national decline, if only just to solidify why they were hucksters and products of poorly thought out ideas. What might be interesting to see would be RD interviews with people whose views might present good motivated by “liberal” religious or civic ideals. If he just goes to 60 Minutes to keep giving the hacks and hucksters currently getting attention and driving us into oblivion he will just keep being more of the same and I will keep on not watching the show he’s joining.

articles.title: Who Are the Good Guys and the Bad Guys? I’m No Longer Sure.
articles.summary: Where does the side of the angels really lie?

comments.name: Spanky Wanky
comments.body: The current system is like the Harlem Globetrotters and the Washington Generals where the only winners are the audience in a sold out show where the rest of us either aren’t allowed to buy a ticket or can’t afford one. So the rational option for the 99% is the nuclear option of radical democratic socialist. I don’t like it. I don’t agree with it.  it. But that’s my view, looking up from the bottom.

comments.name: GWT
comments.body: Democrats MUST take back the Senate to prevent Trump from getting a FOURTH Supreme Court Justice, and for him to effectively be stopped in his tracks for the second half of his term. I don’t care if the Democrat is a socialist or a moderate, we got to make this party take back the Senate!

comments.name: Barry Schiller
comments.body: I've never understood why they use the term Democratic "Socialist" - wouldn't it have been clearer and politically better to use the term "Social Democrats" which implies Scandinavia rather than the Soviet Union and the like that also used the term "socialist"

comments.name: Scientist/Physician
comments.body:
Medicare for all should not be a "socialist"position.  It should be a position supported by all Democrats and accepted as a necessity by Republicans.  Are ALL of the other rich countries in the world "socialist"? No.

Where does the money go in the US Health system?  To pay for insurance company executives, the massive salaries for administrators/bureaucrats in "non-profit" medical centers, and profits in for-profit health companies - not for care of sick people, or to prevent illness.  For example, in my hometown, the President/CEO of a major medical center this year makes over $15 Million, while the nurses and physicians are over-worked and unable to keep up with inflation.  Meanwhile the president of the city's major VA medical center (which is quite good), makes less than $300K.  

Medicare's overhead, real Medicare, not "Advantage Plans", which are really government sponsored for-profit private insurance companies, is less than one-third of the real overhead of Aetna or BlueCross BlueShield.  Patient care is the same. 

Let's stop flushing money down the toilet.  Let's have Medicare for all, and send all of the people making $millions by taking money from our healthcare off to an early retirement. Is this socialism?  No!  It is democracy.

Wake-up Democrats, stop defending the status quo!

comments.name: df
comments.body: They listen to people who have no grey hair anywhere.  They ignore everyone else.

comments.name: Kevin Cahill
comments.body: The Democratic Party must become the party of peace—the party that settles the Ukraine and Iran wars (which we caused), cuts “defense,”  and invests in healthcare and Social Security for the American people.

comments.name: DanielMarcMD
comments.body: Really?? The “people” are telling these candidates they want to abolish the police, do away with the United States Senate, and abolish any US border? Because that is what is on the DSA platform (on their website, if you  assume they aren’t lying about it). No, they aren’t listening to the people. Democratic voters have just fallen for the latest shiny object, like they always do, and this time it is socialism.

comments.name: Johnny99
comments.body: Okay they listen, then do their own thing regardless.

articles.title: Socialists Are Winning Because They Listen to People
articles.summary: Democrats are going to have to organize voters — not just fund-raise off them.

comments.name: LT
comments.body:
Yet another example where second-order consequences were treated as optional — if they were considered at all.

Hormuz disruption leading to global energy shocks and loss of allied trust was as obvious consequence that will reverberate for years.

But perhaps even more damning was the  lack of preparation for modern warfare as demonstrated by Ukraine: drone asymmetry leading to stockpile depletion of expensive weapons. 

$2,000 drones tying up the United States military, depletion of critical weapons that undermine U.S defense interests and commitments. 

Meanwhile Trump demands contractors "hurry-up" too late to matter in the short-term and for the long-term pushes the construction of a "Trump Class" battleship as part of his "Golden Fleet" even referencing 1952 TV show "Victory at Sea".  Price tag: $20 billion — the equivalent of 10,000,000 cheap drones. 

Nobody does strategic incoherence quite like Donald Trump.

comments.name: R7
comments.body: But just a couple weeks after the start, in a prancing press conference, Hegseth boasted that the conflict was already won due to our awesomeness.

comments.name: Pat
comments.body: Prez Trump has revealed his dangerous and absolutely amateur status in terms of strategic thinking. Of course Russia and China are watching and smiling. I

comments.name: GuitarLute
comments.body: After the Hiroshima bomb, Japan did not surrender because they believed the US could only have one weapon. After Nagasaki, the emperor stepped in and surrendered because the 'one and only' weapon theory was wrong. If the Hiroshima bomb had been the only one, Japan never would have surrendered. Similarly, Iran now believes they have taken the worst the US can dish out, and survived (at least the IRGC is intact), so they believe they have won. Well, that is what you get when you hire a fox news commentator to run the conflict and fire most of the experienced military experts.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
Yeah, and people like me were taking note on March 1st.

It's not like it was unknown this was an issue!!

comments.name: Deb
comments.body: Considering Putin plays both sides, was treated to a red-carpet welcome by 47 and tells Iran where to hit our military, we better hope he doesn't decide he wants Alaska back.

comments.name: Carolyn
comments.body: You don’t have to be an “analyst” to know that Moscow and Beijing are loving this fiasco brought on by Hegseth and Trump, with the full blessing of the Republican Party.

comments.name: Grapeview
comments.body:
What are you all worried about? The president said we were loaded with arms.
He wouldn’t tell us a fib about that, would he?

articles.title: The U.S. Is Burning Through Weapons in Iran. Russia and China Are Taking Note.
articles.byline: Anton Troianovski, Jonathan Swan, Eric Schmitt and Julian E. Barnes
articles.summary: The Iran war has depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles, resulting in a significant erosion of firepower. A more drawn-out Iran conflict benefits Moscow and Beijing, some analysts say.

comments.name: monitor
comments.body:
The first time I ever "experienced" South of the Border was on an extremely foggy night traveling on I-95 south.  

We began to see a low glow ahead of us on the highway, as if the fog were going to lift imminently or there was a distant airport or small city ahead. But our maps gave us no clue about what was ahead.  

We continued in the murk at about 10 MPH for seemed like forever.  The glow eventually became a swelling glare and suddenly there was SOTB,  with a few cars creeping up into the parking lot.  We considered stopping but it was very late and we were exhausted.   

But we stopped during daylight on our return north.  The contrast between the pulsing, glowing, 1 a.m. ghost-town and the crazed, gew-gaw powered plastic carnival by day was almost incomprehensible.

comments.name: Peter
comments.body: Sounds great. I don't see myself driving that way anytime soon but it sounds well worth a stop.

comments.name: Ames
comments.body: Stopped there while driving my friend's Ford Granada from Skidmore College in Saratoga Springs NY to Sarasota FL our senior year. We drove nonstop. The billboards, Pedro, the tacos at 2am. Offensive? Better tear down most of Las Vegas and or course, Mar a  Lago, while you're at it.

comments.name: Terri
comments.body: When I was a kid, Dillon, SC, was the Gretna Green for NC teenagers, who ran away to there to get married because even young teens didn’t need parental permission.

comments.name: David
comments.body: I’m surprised the article didn’t mention that former Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke, who grew up a nearby Dillon, was a waiter at South of the Border when he was a teenager.

comments.name: Katherine
comments.body: We loved watching for the billboards along I-95 and we begged our dad to stop every time we drove south. Once we finally did! I can still remember our glee at exploring the place and riding the roller coaster. A generation later, same thing with my kids. Yes, it’s tacky and anachronistic, but it’s a nostalgic gem. I’m delighted to hear that the owners ignored Jim Crow laws, too. Good for them!

comments.name: Suse
comments.body: I had always been told that the owner initially opened up South of the Border to sell kosher essentials for Jewish families traveling from the North to the South. I’m from SC and we took the back roads to the beach and did not stop by South of the Border. I heard about it from many Northern friends along with the Giant Peach and Hilton Head. That’s what they knew about SC.

comments.name: Hutch
comments.body: I have stopped there a lot on trips between Florida and Pennsylvania -- maybe 30-40 times. Tacos are great, rooms are okay and they are pet-friendly, and the fireworks they sell are epic, and the steak house is great. Needless to say, I love South of the Border! Great article. Thank you!

articles.title: Tacky, Rude and Beloved: Is an I-95 Landmark Worth Saving?
articles.summary: South of the Border harks back to a different time in the South, before the region diversified and exploded in growth.

comments.name: IB
comments.body: It depends what you mean by book.  There are many pop books intended to be read lightly for fun that I DNF after hitting the third easy cliche or bad metaphor within the first few pages.  I DFN books where the female character is introduced as a full-on male gaze cliche vessel rather than a person- I've become weary of tolerating this over years and reading hundreds of books. There are other good books I DNF temporarily because I lack the mental leisure to devote, and will pick up later when less real world demands are competing.  I'm guided by Toni Morrison's statement about trusting the author's voice and pacing, but it can become obvious pretty quickly sometimes if that trust is not warranted.  Trust your own tastes and DNF.  Life's too short.

comments.name: Grace
comments.body:
OMG, life is too short to struggle through a book that is just not appealing.  I may give it a few more pages.  When I was younger, I was perhaps more determined to finish - is it something that comes with any wisdom (?) of age.  There is enough pain & suffering & madness in the world - enjoy, enjoy books that speak to you!  I look to reading for pleasure, joy, comfort, escapism, comfort - don't take away the joy I feel in escaping to a good story.  

Perhaps when we pass from this spinning globe there will be a question asking if we each have been a kind, loving person... but I doubt there will be a test question at the pearly gates asking how many books you gave up on finish... overdue library books - maybe!

comments.name: Texan
comments.body: 9 years ago, I happily took a book from NPR’s Book We Love on vacation. The premise was right up my alley. I found it to be long and pretentious. But I stuck with it. I wish I had that time back.

comments.name: Crosstrainer
comments.body: At some point I crossed over from determined to finish to DNF based on whether or not I was enjoying what I was reading,. I use the term “enjoy” widely. It may mean learning about new places, other people’s thoughts and ideas or great plot. But if a book isn’t ticking any of those boxes I will put it down.  Often lately, a strange thing will happen whervim going along fine with a book, well past the half way point, when I suddenly decide, that’s it, and close it for good. Life’s too short to waste time just to be able to say “I read it”.

comments.name: D Casper
comments.body: Too many books, too little time.  DNF is always an option.

comments.name: Bob
comments.body: I’m a book editor and I read as a profession. I likely read 2-3 hours while at work and 2-3 hours daily at home. I’ve come to believe it’s more nuanced than DNF. Not every book is for everyone. But mood, time , etc all play a role. Some of my favorite reading experiences have been putting a book down and returning to it years later and finding the book that was a slog is now incredibly enjoyable. Often because I e become a different reader. I reread books more often as I get older.i do have some guilt around DNF but realistically I know I want to read more than I will ever have time for. At work, different story. I have to triage and figure things out quickly. Often I can figure out if a manuscript is for us in a few minutes.if I like it it may take me a few days to decide as then I do need to keep reading to see if the whole thing works. But my personal reading habits inform my professional. Keep in mind there are millions of not billions of titles published since man started creating books. You’re going to encounter some clunkers.

comments.name: filancia times
comments.body: If I can't get into a book, I usually attribute that to the fact that it's just not the right time for me.  I put it aside and pick it up later, sometimes much later, and usually find I do enjoy it. Sometimes if I'm not into the book, I look at the writing and figure out what it is I don't like.  If the writing is terrible, I have no problem with not continuing.  For me, it's almost always " wring book, wrong time."

comments.name: East Of Cicero
comments.body: I'm usually reading a few books at once, so if a book doesn't keep me hooked by page 70, I'll abandon it and simply forget about it. To be fair, as I get older I also forget whatever book I read three books ago, so it may not matter if I finish a book or not. There's always another one to read.

articles.title: How DNF Became A-OK
articles.summary: Is it shameful, or sensible, to put down a book you don’t enjoy? Three little letters, and social media, have turbocharged a longstanding debate.

articles.title: The ‘Jury Duty’ Scam That Cost This Family $25,000
articles.byline: Joe Barrett | Photography by Megan May for WSJ
articles.summary: In a growing ruse, swindlers pose as cops and use tremendous pressure to trap people, including young professionals.

comments.name: Andrew Dance
comments.body: You get what you pay for. Don't ever buy "refurbished" anything unless you know how to either factory reset or reformat it thoroughly. Even then, I'd say just get a new device from authorized stores. Or you can just use your current one unless it is broken.

comments.name: James Joseph
comments.body: Scam calls seem to come in groups then nothing for a long while. Never answer a call from an unknown number, never answer from a number that you are not expecting a call from, and block all unknown numbers that do not leave a message.  I commend Kimberly Fudge for her willingness to discuss this situation candidly, maybe her story will help someone avoid the same ordeal.

comments.name: Paul P
comments.body: Never answer a call from a number that you do not recognize.  Let them leave a message.

comments.name: TIFFANY ONEAL
comments.body: I live in Tampa and this exact scam was attempted on me last week! I smelled a rat before the male caller extracted any money or personal info from me but it was scary that they knew my name, phone, address, and after speaking with them in real time, that I am female. It was unnerving and I feel surprisingly shaken and so sad that this is the world we live in now.

comments.name: Mark T
comments.body: I once had a call from an 'agent of the IRS" who said I owed money to the IRS for late taxes. I told him I wanted to call the IRS to confirm, he gave me his name and then I called the IRS. Had to wait about a half hour to get finally they, turned out I owed nothing.

comments.name: Gregory Clark
comments.body:
I have a relative who called me last week when she was in the middle of an attempted scam. She got a call from the FTC that someone somewhere had downloaded dirty pictures and paid for them using her credit card. My relative said that she mentioned to the “FTC” that she should call her credit union and financial adviser and alert them to what was going on. The “FTC” person said “There’s no need to do that, we can clear this up on our own”.

My relative expressed frustration that she had to deal with all this because of the alleged credit card transaction, i.e. she didn’t realize she was being scammed. I told her to stop talking to these people and to immediately call her credit union, financial adviser, and police. 

My relative is renowned for her lack of street smarts, and I’m guessing the woman in the article is also lacking in this regard. How do you fix this? I don’t know. In each case a better knowledge of government and how it operates would have stopped things sooner, but educating people about this is for a number of reasons not an easy fix.

comments.name: Amy Molieri
comments.body: If I don't recognize the number,  I never pick up. Period. I don't care who it is. Leave a voicemail. I won't call back unless it's from someone I am expecting a call from. Even then, I check the number before calling back. One thing I learned is never record your voice on your voicemail. Scammers can use it to open accounts and use your recorded name. Use an auto one. Same thing with text messages.  I don't respond I just delete.

comments.name: Lawrence Karch
comments.body:
Basically, the deal is this. If you get a telephone call, or maybe an email, that threatens you with some kind of legal action, simply ignore it. Even if the caller knows your email and some amount in your savings/checking account, just hang up.

Anything that serious that it would involve law enforcement to be involved would notify you using the USPS.

Of course any phone call/email that involves you sending money to someone should automatically signal scam to you.

comments.name: Joe Jensen
comments.body: Hopefully when the rubber hits the road - the general election, Democrats can set aside their differences and unite behind the chosen candidate on the ballot.  The main objective - the only objective - is to win the election and flip both the Senate and the House of Representatives.  After that is accomplished, let the policy squabbles resume!  Too many times Democratic voters have not voted because the featured candidate does not represent all their ideological aspirations, and the other side wins.  Makes you wish we had a parliamentary form of government where different constituencies can be effectively represented.  Nevertheless, given what we have, vote BLUE!

comments.name: JoeDMplsMN
comments.body: The train wreck that is our current political morass has been coming for a long time.  Trump merely took advantage of a moribund institution, the federal government.  Contrary to the Republican Party’s myopic view, the U.S. is very large and very diverse.  And sadly the current Democratic Party doesn’t fully appreciate it either.  We are living through a period of unprecedented, dynamic change.   Yet, our Federal government is at best, old, slow and unresponsive, much of that now institutionalized.  It is also ripe for the corruption outside money buys. I applaud El-Sayed and other progressives.  But, in order to fully return the national government to “we the people” we need to first strengthen and secure our state institutions  and build new national coalitions from there.  It can not be done from the top down.

comments.name: MisterCamera
comments.body:
Let's be real. The truth is, the current "ruling" Democrats ARE BOUGHT. Just like the old Republicans pre-Trump WERE BOUGHT. Culturally, there is night and day between America's DSA and it's ALT and Far Right. But the wide area that both agreed on before Trump was that they were tired of being taken for a ride by politicians who made political and economic promises and never delivered. EXCEPT FOR DONORS AND CORPORATIONS. The thing that has united Americans more than anything is the belief that the government, laws, and economy are rigged by those with vast wealth and power. And that those interests have become so parasitic that they are just vacuuming all of the wealth and economic opportunity, to the point you are only a spectator in your own life. And you have no real choices. Economic and social mobility has come to a standstill. All of this is simultaneously true with the social and cultural split and differences in America that vote are just as apt to fight about.

Republican voters have decided that if they are stuck with corruption on both sides, they will settle for getting the cultural side of their agenda. Which the far right and Trump are giving them in ways they never got it before. That is why he is popular despite members of his own party thinking he is super corrupt. They figure at least they are getting SOME of what they want vs NOTHING before.

Which is why Democrats are OK with the DSA now. They see them as ACTION politicians. Like Trump.

comments.name: Publius
comments.body: The fundamental brokenness of the USA for most Americans has been on full display this entire century, where the voter quest for outsiders to fix it has persisted from Obama through Trump.  What has changed is the obviousness with which controlling oligarchs manifest their economic and political power, which under Trump has included simple removal of means of civic participation.  The republic of 1789 is gone, yet the mechanics of a zombie state persist.  The next ten years may demonstrate what replacement(s) may arise.

comments.name: Captain Boner
comments.body:
The Republican party of Lincoln freed the slaves that were under the thumb of the southern Democrats, then a Republican (Hayes) abandoned Reconstruction to placate Democrats in order to gain the presidency

Under Wilson, a 20th century Democrat, racism remained a prominent feature.  

Then the 20th century GOP under Harding and Coolidge came along with deregulaiton and lower taxes to please big busness, until the Depression demanded change in the eyes of the voters.

The modern Democratic party was a product of FDR's New Deal to support workers, a WWII victory over fascism, and the pursuit of Civil Rights under LBJ.  The Vietnam War soured the Democratic vibe, leading to the reign of a Republican president who was forced to resign. 

When the nation switched to a Dem president and (unfairly) blamed Carter for inflation, and Reagan handed the country over to the billionaires, the Democrats suddenly shifted into a more conservative mode, despite the agitations of a financially well-supported Tea Party and MAGA.

The result is a GOP leader telling everybody how great the economy is while Amazon warehouse workers are abused like slaves, and the Democratic Party that used to lift up the abused workers is becoming harder to find a role for.

And now that the Court is what it is, how much does it really matter at this juncture?

Money in politics has increasingly, over the decades, poisoned the mission of both parties and all 3 branches of government.  The DSA will do the same.

comments.name: Dabney L
comments.body: Stevens was only able to whiff at the nomination thanks to more than $60 million in outside spending from the democratic establishment status quo: the DCCC led by Schumer, the DNC, corporate PAC money and most astoundingly, nearly $30 million from AIPAC and affiliated groups. The Stevens campaign outspent Al-Sayed nearly ten to one. Without all the fear mongering about Abdul being a scary Muslim, he would have stomped in the primary. Count me among the former democrats who feel abandoned by the party. I am now firmly in the camp of progressive and DSA candidates who refuse PAC money, refuse to engage in cultural wedge issues to distract and divide us, and advocate for a basic social safety net that includes universal healthcare, affordable housing and childcare, and a livable minimum wage.

comments.name: Patrick Weidinger
comments.body: We are not listening because we have learned to ignore so-called media pundits who have been wrong over and over and over and over again. Media pundits determined to convince Americans that this candidate or that party is "unelectable".

comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
As we drift into the second six months of Trump's "Special Military Operation", this election is going to be about its effects on the economy.

With the Straights essentially closed since the start of the war, fuel prices (and i mean gas, diesel, heating oil) have been held in check by a few items like China's cut back in purchases, the Strategic Oil Reserve releases, and excess capacity that was there before the war started.

All of that is now running out.  So let's say there is a scenario where gas is $6/gallon, diesel and heating oil at $7 a gallon with all of the run-on inflation effects of such prices.

This election is going to be about economics. Bond market-driven interest rates, groceries, the increases in Part D premiums for seniors, another 8-10% increase in insurance premiums are all pointing to very bad news for the economy.

And we have the most unpopular - and getting more so - president in memory?

This is what is going to drive voters and I'm not sure that the huge Republican war chest and AIPAC can beat back America's anger.

articles.title: Hello, Democrats? Are You Listening?
articles.byline: Jamelle Bouie, Michelle Cottle, Michael Duffy, Derek Arthur and Rochelle Widdowson
articles.summary: Michigan presents as much a warning as it does an opportunity.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body: The political calculus will have the two parties creating such a void in the middle that a moderate party will be created and most citizens will gladly join together, creating a stronger third party than D or R. It's inevitable.

comments.name: CB Evans
comments.body:
Anderson has spent a good deal of time and thought on the subject of a national breakup, so he certainly has more expertise than I.

But to me, a "breakup" is an entirely silly notion. Even the most "red" or "blue" states have hundreds of thousands up to many millions of voters from the other side of the spectrum.

How, exactly, would it work? States choose which federation to join, then mass migration? 

Barring war, I don't see this happening.

comments.name: Paul Wortman no
comments.body: It's been clear for some time that Lincoln's project of Reconstruction has failed, and there are two Americas: the Union, now blue states, and the Confederacy, now red states--one democratic, pluralistic, and egalitarian, and the other authoritarian, oligarchic, and racist. The initial wound of slavery embedded in our founding document has never healed, resulting in endless conflict and bitter divisiveness. It's time to ask the voters in the states to vote on partition into a Democratic Union of America and a Confederation of America.

comments.name: Robert Cole
comments.body: The one sentence that really struck me in this thoughtful opinion is this: “The century of relative domestic tranquillity between the Civil War and civil rights depended on the awful compromise of Jim Crow.” Controversial maybe, but definitely insightful. As I have been saying for quite a while now, Lincoln made a mistake allowing the confederate states to rejoin the U.S., the result being that the South won the Civil War.

comments.name: N. Smith
comments.body: Anybody with a shred of memory knows it hasn't always this way. Sure, Republicans and Democrats were different from each other and didn't always see eye to eye -- that's been true ever since this country's inception. But the anger, hate and sheer hostility that leads to open violence is new. And it's ugly. Sorry, but I'll just come out and say it. To a large extent, all this has accelerated within the last decade, which happens to coincide with Donald Trump's ascension to the political stage. His rallies were legend when it came to him provoking the crowd into attacking those who didn't agree with him; and then, there was January 6th. A decade of hate and fearmongering has had a deleterious effect on the country. Can we survive it? .....I sincerely hope so.

comments.name: Paul S.
comments.body: I’m thinking that both sides should agree to amend the Constitution to add a “ notwithstanding” clause similar to that in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.  Too complicated to explain in detail here, but basically it allows a province to adopt a law that violates the Charter, except for laws that infringe on a list of specific rights that are designated as “fundamental.” There would of course be arguments about what should be included in that list, but as a resident of a blue state I’d be ok giving up, for example, a federal right to abortion in exchange for a system that would allow my state to override the Second Amendment when it comes to gun regulation.

comments.name: RedOctBlue
comments.body:
I disagree with the premise that America is fundamentally divided into two increasingly incompatible camps. I think our political system is doing a remarkably good job of making Americans feel more divided than they actually are.

By and large, Americans share many of the same fundamental values—family, freedom, security, opportunity, fairness and a better future for their children. We differ over which values we emphasize and, more importantly, how we believe government should pursue them. That is disagreement, not necessarily societal rupture.

The real problem is our system of governance. A two-party, winner-take-all system gives politicians enormous incentives to turn every difference into an existential conflict. They deepen our distrust of one another because division is politically useful to them.

The comparison with the 19th century also has limits. The country then was divided over slavery—a genuinely heinous institution that went to the very foundation of what America was. Today’s political disagreements, however bitter, are fundamentally different.

Perhaps we should stop asking how to reconcile two Americas and start asking why our governing system continually produces the illusion that there are two Americas that cannot live together.

The country may not need to be divided less. Our political system needs to be changed so that ordinary differences don’t have to become political warfare.

To be sure, the crisis she highlights is real. The states she visited are among the hardest places to live in the country, offering social safety nets weaker than those in many developing nations. My husband was hit first and landed in the gutter, bones broken, bleeding, screaming in pain. He took the brunt of the impact while I suffered minor cuts and bruises. The driver said she didn't see us (it was 10a on a sunny morning in February), told the police officer that her cell phone was in the trunk (hard to believe). We badgered our city council person and department of transportation for a Pedestrian Interval Delay and got one after several years. It is lifesaving and reduces my post-traumatic stress but not my vigilance. Drivers are increasing distracted, reckless, self absorbed, i.e., running red lights, making u-turns in the middle of the street, turning before pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk. We are now 69, still walking daily, active and agile, walking at a quick pace, no hearing loss, no mobility issues. Despite the usual "the US is to blame" for all of Cuba's woes, Cuba's economic woes cannot be attributed solely to the U.S. embargo. While the embargo inflicts massive financial damage on Cuba, an overwhelming consensus among economists, historians, and international analysts indicates that internal systemic failures, central planning inefficiencies, and extreme import dependence act as severe structural bottlenecks.

The Inefficiencies of Central Planning: State control over the vast majority of economic sectors discourages domestic innovation, suppresses productivity, and creates severe bureaucratic red tape.Decimated Domestic Production: Cuba suffers from chronic food and fuel shortages because it produces less than 40% of its needed fuel and relies heavily on imported food. Decades of state-managed agriculture have failed to make the island self-sufficient.Infrastructure Collapse: Decades of underinvestment and deferred maintenance have left Cuba’s electrical grid, water networks, and public transport system on the brink of total collapse.Currency and Inflation Crises: Ill-fated domestic monetary reforms—such as the elimination of the dual-currency system—triggered runaway hyperinflation, devastating the purchasing power of ordinary citizens.

Amazon delivery trucks are getting rid of the annoying traditional beepers that emit a pure single-frequency tone that penetrates into buildings. The new, less annoying, backup tone is a broadband white-noise sound (called BBS-Tek or a multi-frequency alarm) that allows pedestrians to more easily determine where the sound is coming from.

Compared to the traditional beeper sound, the new multi-frequency sound dissipates rapidly outside the immediate backup danger zone, confining the warning sound to only those nearby pedestrians that may be at risk. And, from personal experience, I can say that when I hear the new sound, it is much less annoying than the traditional beeper.

Moreover, the new device can automatically adjust its decibel level relative to the ambient noise level in the surrounding environment. The system is designed to consistently set its sound level to roughly 5 to 10 decibels above background noise by sampling the ambient noise environment about twice a second.

Apparently, many other private and government vehicles are transitioning to the less annoying and safer multi-frequency backup warning devices.

Spirituality or Exploitation?

Look at some of the “spiritual” communities emerging in Turkey, especially along the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts. You often find bearded, fit men in their 50s or 60s, dressed in loose linen and posing as spiritual guides, or middle-aged women with a calm, mystical image. Their education and professional backgrounds often have little to do with the authority they claim.
 Then come frame drums, ney flutes, dim lights, whirling rituals, breathing exercises and talk of “energy,” “vibrations,” “healing” and “consciousness.” Rhythmic movement and an intense atmosphere can create temporary relief, which is then sold as “spiritual transformation” or “healing.”

This is where exploitation begins.
Using the loneliness, fears, vulnerability and need for belonging of troubled people to bind them to a group—and then charging for retreats, sessions, workshops and rituals—is not spirituality. It is spiritual abuse.
I say this as someone raised in a Muslim family in Turkey who has visited Mevlânâ Celâleddîn-i Rûmî’s lodge in Konya many times. If you want to understand Jalal al-Din Rumi, read his works and study the Mevlevi tradition. Using his name, Sufi symbols and “universal love” to market dubious healing practices is something else entirely.
I no longer believe in such practices. I trust science, reason and critical thinking—evidence-based ways of understanding the human mind and body.

comments.name: Steven Reidbord MD

Well done! Finally a piece in the NYT that delves into the complexity of our field, doesn’t pit one faction against another, and addresses the false narrative of “evidence based treatment.”

I too have discussed these issues with Drs Ogden and Shedler, and although they are very different people, each offers an important corrective for our devolving field. Dr Solm’s efforts to combine psychoanalysis and brain science, a task first attempted by Freud, is ultimately the path forward. Yours is a hopeful and impressively comprehensive article that I hope many readers take to heart.

comments.name: Writer & Therapist
comments.body:
As a therapist and candidate in psychoanalytic training, I was thrilled to read this piece. While I think gatekeeping is often problematic, there needs to be some sort of gatekeeping in entering this field. It is terrifyingly easy to be become a licensed psychotherapist. Graduate schools do barely scratch the surface on adequately training students, as Dr. Duane stated, the quality of post-graduate training is inconsistent at best, and many clinicians have ever been in their own therapy. High-caliber clinical supervision at group practices and community mental health centers is often lacking. We end up with a generation of therapists who have not been prepared for this work, and whose unaddressed personal issues unknowingly seep into the therapy room.

The other factor here is accessibility. It is rarely sustainable for therapists to maintain a practice accepting health insurance, and most people cannot afford to pay out-of-pocket. We as therapists are caught in the middle of this, where we eventually have to choose between providing affordable care and our own livelihood.

You castigate (correctly) the so-called scientific viability of CBT, and vastly verbalize the validity of your own psychoanalytic approach. Yes the research shows that client-therapist relationship matters the most. As a Gestalt-trained psychotherapist in practice for 20 years, I agree. I myself have contemplated writing a book on our experience with the US therapy, psychology and adjoining insurance infrastructure. 
This is the best piece I’ve seen written about frustrations with therapy, particularly the insurance piece. Finding a decent therapist among all the options in your area is daunting to put it nicely. Reviews are non-existent - who’s going to put their name in a review for a therapist? What’s the right “modality” for your child’s symptoms (what is even a modality?) Turns out the therapist you found that seems good is out of network, darn. The one you finally find that your child connects with eventually admits they’ve reached a point where their area of focus can’t take your child any further. I can go on and on and on. 

It’s is a practice that needs help. Meanwhile the patients, particularly teens, are impacted most.

What I have never seen, ever, in any reporting, is a cost breakdown of expenses. Labor costs are one of the most transparent expenses, as the contracts are collectively bargained and easily found. What isn’t transparent are things like venue rentals and fees. All Broadway houses are owned by a small group; setting aside the 6 theaters owned by nonprofit theater companies and 1 owned by the city and operated by Disney, the remaining 34 are owned by just 3 companies and, in fact, half are owned by just one. These companies collect rent from productions, cuts of the box office, cuts from concessions, fees from vendors, and add additional fees to tickets that go straight to them as profits. That major owner, the Shubert Organization, also owns Telecharge, the major theatrical ticketing platform. These entities are also producing entities, which means in many cases they have vertically integrated nearly all aspects of the production and are also party to union negotiations! The Broadway houses always win and yet their operations are not typically transparent and certainly never investigated or interrogated.

My Aquatic Epiphany

Funny thing happened early last Monday morning at as I plopped myself into a big pool inside an even bigger gym. 
Suddenly I found myself thrown back more than 70 years, into my neighborhood’s high school pool where my mother was beginning to give me and my best friend Norman our first swimming lesson.
While I was totally, giddily psyched up, Norman was totally psyched out, pale as a ghost, shivering, then telling us, “I’d rather be a live coward than a dead hero.”
Then, as suddenly as I’d been catapulted back there, I was catapulted forward to the present, as I waved goodbye to my mom, Norman and myself. Then I smiled, sighed and began my swim.

Norman & I went our separate ways yet stayed close.  
I became the godfather of his first son.
Norman joined the fire department in his fast- growing community to serve strangers by saving their lives at any time, in any way he possibly could.

He passed away about twenty-five years ago and was buried with a hero’s salute for his career of selfless bravery that included an official ceremony in his honor by his entire department and those of all other area fire companies at his burial site that extended their tallest ladders as a canopy for the motorcade that passed beneath them.

I'll always feel buoyed up by that special memory.

Thanks to all those Metro Diarists from The Stoop for their wise advice and continued encouragement to swim back into the future.

I promise not to bore you anymore about it!

Clara Ester (78) 
Was With Martin Luther King Jr. in His Last Moments

A Memphis college student and activist, she witnessed Dr. King’s assassination in 1968 when he was shot at his motel and ran to him to check his pulse.
Dr. King’s death, she said, forever changed her life. 
“I know that I was no longer the same person I had been,” she wrote in her 2016 essay.
After she received a bachelor’s degree in elementary school education from LeMoyne-Owen College in Memphis, Ms. Ester soon left Tennessee and lived her final 50 years or so in Mobile, where she became a lay minister and ran a community center.

In Mobile, she devoted herself to justice, compassion and reconciliation, becoming a deaconess, or lay minister, in the United Methodist Church and the executive director of a community center. At the center, she oversaw programs that assisted the blind, the deaf, and homeless mothers and children; operated night classes for students seeking their high school equivalency diploma; and collected toys for Christmas.

May her memory be a blessing.

Plenty of time to scroll through the Times. Plenty of time to remember times past. The day stretches out like a cat. Take care, friends of the stoop! Dolce fa niente.

In the first move, she bends forward before stepping up which puts a lot of strain on the knee joint.  This is true with climbing stairs as well. I recently learned from someone who does physical therapy with people over 50 to rethink the way you climb stairs.

Be very careful not to lean backward, but when you go upstairs, stand a bit straighter and push up with the back foot to engage the calf and take some of the load off the knee joint.  It takes a little conscious thinking to get the coordination just right, but this change helps a lot if you have bad knees.

But what I see is that people want climate change addressed but complain that Europeans do not use aircon as commonly as the US. 
Others write about how the world is becoming too crowded, accelerating climate change, but then complain that the birth rate is too low. 
The best  that scientists hope for is that the rate of climate change can be slowed. We have to live with what we have now, and the world has always survived. 
By the way, Australians travel extensively in the Europe in the shoulder seasons and the winter. Others may follow our lead. 
My last word, it is unrealistic to expect people to cut back dramatic on travelling. My country has half the population with a parent born overseas and while people can afford to travel to visit extended family they will.

Whereas Scaramucci is the polar opposite - wild, un-filtered and intelligent enough to make himself the butt of the joke from time to time.  And he’s the one who knows how this sinister, capricious Trump world operates and, of equal importance, how the money influences it.  She brings the intellectual and analytical  heft, he brings the receipts.  And they are both funny in their own inimitable way.  So you end up with this oddball, trans-Atlantic pairing where it’s scones and clotted cream versus Dunkin Donuts every week, which is what  gives the show its peculiar charm.
